name: Interrogative Use of Indeterminates

dimensions.form: Full indeterminate series; non-subject interrogative phrases are normally fronted, while interrogative subjects remain in basic position and echoes may remain in situ
dimensions.meaning: The open variable is packaged as a request for its value
dimensions.function: Marks the focus of the question; question-answer congruence
dimensions.distribution: Main and subordinate open interrogatives; main-clause inversion follows a fronted non-subject, while subordinate interrogatives and interrogative subjects normally retain subject–verb order

1.definition: Asks for the value of the indeterminate's open variable, constraining its sort
1.details: All members of the indeterminate series participate in this packaging

examples.note: Interrogative subject in basic subject position; no subject–auxiliary inversion

constraints.description: The interrogative property percolates from the indeterminate to its phrase and clause. Non-subject phrases are normally fronted and trigger subject–auxiliary inversion in main clauses; subjects are not fronted, subordinate clauses normally do not invert, and echoes may leave the phrase in situ.

projection.target: In Whose coat did Jo borrow?, the whole phrase whose coat fronts while whose supplies the open variable for the possessor. With an interrogative subject, Who left? has no corresponding auxiliary inversion.
projection.evidence: CGEL separates the interrogative feature of a word from that of its containing phrase and tests subject versus non-subject distributions.

curious.title: Question words
curious.summary: Who, what, where, when, why, how and their relatives mark a question by asking for the missing piece of information.
curious.body:
A question word asks for the value of something left open. Whose book asks about the owner, and Who came asks about a person. Each word limits what kind of answer fits: a person, a place, a time.

Question words normally come first in the question, as in Whose coat did Jo borrow? When the question word is the subject, as in Who left?, it stays in its usual place and the verb needn't move. A question inside a longer sentence, such as I wonder where she went, keeps ordinary word order.
curious.try: Turn Jo borrowed the red coat into a question about the colour, then into a question about whose coat it was. Where did your question word end up?

teacher.summary: Covers wh-words used to ask questions, including where they go and whether the verb moves.
teacher.explain: In this packaging, a member of the indeterminate series asks for the value of its open variable, constraining its sort. The interrogative property passes from the word to its phrase and clause. Non-subject phrases are normally fronted and trigger subject-auxiliary inversion in main clauses. Subjects are not fronted, so Who left? has no inversion, and subordinate interrogatives normally keep subject-verb order, as in I wonder where she went. In Whose coat did Jo borrow?, the whole phrase whose coat fronts while whose supplies the open variable for the possessor. Echo questions may leave the phrase in its original position. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditionally called wh-words or interrogative pronouns, adverbs and determiners. This dictionary groups them as interrogative uses of the indeterminate series.

contrasts.note: A fronted non-subject phrase; subject and auxiliary swap places.

watch_for: A learner might invert the subject and verb in Who left?
A learner might invert in the subordinate question I wonder where she went.
teacher.activity: Students turn statements into questions about each part, then sort them by whether the question word is the subject, and note when the verb order changes.

child.hook: What do question words ask for?
child.explain: Question words ask for the missing piece. Who asks about a person. Where asks about a place. The question word normally comes first.
child.play: Pick a sentence like "Jo borrowed a coat." Ask a question about each part of it, using who, what or whose. What would each answer be?
